en.sup: Supplied in English. Our Greek text has no verb in this clause: 'and he rich'.

01.r: Joins the new character to the scene.
01.n: The setting comes from the verse before; this verse does not name the town.

02.r: Draws attention to the man about to be named.

03.r: An adult male, introduced before his name.
03.n: Abbott-Smith defines this word as 'a man, Lat. vir': a male, as against a woman or a boy, not the general word for a human being.

04.n: The noun 'name' in the dative, 'by name'. With 'called' it makes a doubled expression, 'called by name', which the ASV and YLT keep and the others shorten to 'named'.

05.n: A present passive participle, literally 'being called'.

06.n: Abbott-Smith gives the Hebrew form זַכַּי, Zaccai, compares the same name in Nehemiah, and describes him as 'a publican'.

07.r: Adds the first fact about him.

08.r: Zacchaeus, the subject of what follows.
08.n: Abbott-Smith notes that this pronoun is always emphatic in the nominative unless the article comes before it. How much weight 'he' carries here is a matter of reading; it may do little more than keep the focus on Zacchaeus.

10.r: A man over other toll collectors.
10.n: Abbott-Smith defines it as 'a chief tax-collector, chief publican' and records it only in this verse. This study renders it 'chief toll collector' to keep it with τελώνης. The Geneva's 'the chiefe receiuer of the tribute' brings in 'tribute', which this study keeps for φόρος.
t: the chiefe receiuer of the tribute

11.r: Adds the second fact about him.

12.r: Zacchaeus again, now as the one who is rich.
12.n: The Textus Receptus reads 'this (man)' here; see the note on the text.

14.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'rich, wealthy' and cites this verse. That his wealth came from his post is a reasonable reading of the verse's pairing of the two facts, but it is not stated.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads 'and this man was rich' (καὶ οὗτος ἦν πλούσιος), with οὗτος, 'this', for our second αὐτός and an added ἦν, 'was'. The KJV's 'and he was rich' renders that verb; our text has none, so this study supplies 'was' in italics.
